q: בת 73, מגיעה למיון עקב קוצר נשימה. היא מתארת החמרה במצבה בחודש האחרון, עם קוצר נשימה, ירידה תפקודית, וסחרחורת במאמץ מינימאלי מזה כשבוע. אושפזה בחצי שנה האחרונה 6 פעמים עקב קוצר נשימה, כאבים בחזה ובצקות פריפריות. ברקע - מחלת לב איסכמית, מחלת כלי דם היקפיים, היצרות עורק כלייתי, סוכרת. עברה ניתוח מעקפים לפני כ- 10 שנים, וצנתור אחרון במשך אשפוזה האחרון עם התערבות למעקפים ופתיחתם, כמו כן הושתל סטנט לעורק כלייתי המוצר. בבדיקה- לחץ דם 110/70, דופק 130, נשימות 24, מעבדה- BUN 23, קריאטינין 1.5 בהחמרה מבסיס. אקוקרדיוגרפיה הראתה חדר שמאל מורחב עם מקטע פליטה 20% ואי ספיקה מיטראלית קלה. איזו מההתערבויות הבאות יכולה לשפר את איכות חייה ולהאריך אותם?
o: השתלת לב
מכשיר תומך בחדר שמאל Left ventricular assisted device
הזלפת תכשירים אינוטרופיים כגון DOBUTAMINE או MILRINONE
אין מה שיכול לשפר את מצבה, יש להעבירה לטיפול פליאטיבי בלבד
explanation:
The stem describes **advanced heart failure** with markedly reduced EF, repeated admissions, functional decline, dizziness and worsening renal function despite revascularization; it does not state that medical therapy has been optimized. An **LVAD assessment** is reasonable because selected patients with severe HF can gain symptom, quality-of-life and survival benefits, including destination therapy when transplantation is unsuitable. Optimal medical treatment and individual suitability must first be assessed (p. 1189).

**A. Heart transplantation.** Wrong, this is not the official choice. Age and comorbidity limit suitability in this case, but age alone does not automatically exclude transplantation (p. 1190).
**B. A left ventricular assist device.** Correct, an LVAD may improve symptoms, quality of life and survival in selected patients with severe HF, addressing both outcomes requested, subject to suitability assessment (p. 1189).
**C. Infusion of dobutamine or milrinone.** Wrong, infusions can relieve symptoms in selected patients, but have not been shown to improve outcomes and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias; they do not provide the survival benefit sought (p. 1189).
**D. Nothing can improve her condition; provide palliative care alone.** Wrong, palliative care belongs within treatment and goal assessment, but rejecting every possible advanced-treatment benefit is unjustified given potential LVAD benefit in a suitable patient (p. 1189).

Transplantation is not the official choice. Suitability is limited by this age and comorbidity, but automatic exclusion based on age alone is not justified; the book describes favorable outcomes in carefully selected older patients (p. 1190).
Choosing an LVAD means referral for specialist assessment, inferred from the vignette and source treatment options, not an instruction to implant without assessing suitability (p. 1189).
Suitability is not automatic: specialist assessment must include comorbidity, frailty, goals of care and risks of bleeding, infection, stroke and thrombosis (Hazzard 8e, p. 1189).
Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1189-1190.

q: בת 86, התקבלה למחלקת סיעוד מורכב עקב פצע לחץ דרגה 4 עמוק ומזוהם באזור הסאקרום. קיבלה טיפול מקומי בפצע באמצעות ניקוי והסרת הרקמות הנימקיות. כעבור שבועיים עדיין הפרשה מרובה עם ריח אופנסיבי, סימני צלוליטיס מסביב, ללא חום סיסטמי. בספירת דם 13,000 לויקוציטים, CRP = 24.5 (תקין עד 0.5). נלקח מטוש לתרבית עם צמיחה של Pseudomonas aeruginosa ו- Providencia. מה הטיפול המתאים במצב זה?
o: טיפול מקומי בפצע בלבד. אין צורך בטיפול אנטיביוטי
אנטיביוטיקה רחבת טווח
טיפול אנטיביוטי סיסטמי מותאם לרגישות החיידקים שצמחו
הטיפול ב VAC (לחץ שלילי) הוא טיפול הבחירה בפצע מזוהם
explanation:
Distinguish **clinical infection** of a pressure injury from organisms found on its surface. A superficial culture is insufficient for selecting treatment of deep infection; broad coverage is discussed when bacteremia is suspected, pending appropriate cultures (Hazzard 8e, pp. 695, 697). Absence of fever does not exclude significant infection in an older adult, but the stem does not establish bacteremia (p. 1669; clinical inference).
"Do not rely on cultures of the wound surface or wound drainage; they will present only the surface contamination." (p. 695)

**A. Local wound treatment alone, without antibiotics.** Wrong, according to the key. Cellulitis and persistent local deterioration raise concern for spreading infection. The source discusses systemic antibiotics for infection with systemic manifestations and assessment despite absent fever in older adults (pp. 697, 1669; inference).
**B. Broad-spectrum antibiotics.** Correct, according to the key. The source supports coverage of several organism groups when pressure-injury bacteremia is suspected, before appropriate culture results. Coverage should not automatically be narrowed on the basis of a superficial swab alone (pp. 695, 697).
**C. Systemic antibiotics tailored to the organisms grown from the swab.** Wrong, a superficial swab does not establish the deep pathogens; the source warns against basing antibiotic selection on misleading surface cultures (pp. 695, 1668).
**D. VAC as the treatment of choice for an infected wound.** Wrong, negative-pressure therapy reduces wound volume as an adjunct to debridement and other care; it does not replace treatment of the infection driving this decision (p. 697).

"Official IMA key: ב. IMA 2021-Dec Subspecialty official answer key, Q82. The conflicting bank explanation is hidden."

A superficial swab is not a reliable basis for antibiotic selection for deep infection. With systemic infection signs, empirical treatment should reflect the clinical condition and appropriate cultures (Hazzard 8e, pp. 697, 1668).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 695, 697, 1668–1669.

q: Which paired changes in the male sexual response with aging are listed in Hazzard?
o: Higher ejaculatory volume and a shorter refractory period
Lower ejaculatory volume and a shorter refractory period
Lower ejaculatory volume and a longer refractory period
Higher ejaculatory volume and a longer refractory period
explanation:
Hazzard lists **lower ejaculatory volume** and a **longer refractory period** among age-related changes in the male sexual response. These are separate aspects of the response cycle, so both directions must match the table (p. 549, Table 37-1).
"Lower ejaculatory volume" (p. 549).
"Lengthening of the refractory period" (p. 549).

**A. Higher ejaculatory volume and a shorter refractory period.** Wrong, neither direction matches: the table describes lower volume and lengthening of the refractory period (p. 549).
**B. Lower ejaculatory volume and a shorter refractory period.** Wrong, volume decreases as stated, but the refractory period lengthens rather than shortens (p. 549).
**C. Lower ejaculatory volume and a longer refractory period.** Correct, both the volume change and refractory-period change match the listed age-related pattern (p. 549).
**D. Higher ejaculatory volume and a longer refractory period.** Wrong, lengthening of the refractory period is consistent with the table, but increased ejaculatory volume is not (p. 549).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 549.
ref: Hazzard Ch 37 — SEXUALITY , SEXUAL FUNCTION, AND THE AGING MAN

q: An 83-year-old woman with depression has a partial response and adverse effects during antidepressant treatment. After clinical reassessment, she and her clinician agree on a medication change. Which principle should guide dose selection and adjustment?
o: Select a target dose from the usual range despite troublesome adverse effects
Start at the full target dose and escalate rapidly for inadequate response
Adjust the dose to individual response, adverse effects, safety, and drug interactions
Set the effective dose from age and weight before assessing treatment response
explanation:
**Antidepressant dosing** is individualized rather than fixed by a universal therapeutic window (p. 1015). Hazzard states: "the best dosage is not a number fixed in stone, but rather the dosage that works for that individual patient" and "Safety, side effects, and interactions will dictate the maximum dosage" (p. 1015). It also favors slow titration rather than beginning at a full dose (p. 1015).

**A. Select a target dose from the usual range despite troublesome adverse effects.** Wrong, the source makes side effects and safety limits part of dose selection. Persisting toward a generic target despite troublesome effects disregards those limits (p. 1015).
**B. Start at the full target dose and escalate rapidly for inadequate response.** Wrong, the source recommends planning slow upward titration rather than starting at a full dosage. A full-dose start with rapid escalation does not follow that approach (p. 1015).
**C. Adjust the dose to individual response, adverse effects, safety, and drug interactions.** Correct, this combines the individual response with the factors that limit dosage in the source. It does not presume that a particular dose is effective or tolerable for every patient (p. 1015).
**D. Set the effective dose from age and weight before assessing treatment response.** Wrong, the source defines the best dosage by what works for the individual and by safety, adverse effects, and interactions. Age and weight without response assessment do not supply that individualized judgment (p. 1015).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1015.
ref: Hazzard Ch 65 — MAJOR DEPRESSION· Harrison Ch 50 — Unintentional Weight Loss

q: A 91-year-old man with Parkinson disease, falls, and orthostatic hypotension takes amitriptyline for pain. The team has decided to remove an antidepressant with strong anticholinergic activity. Which plan accomplishes this under Beers 2023?
o: Replace amitriptyline with imipramine for continued pain management
Discontinue amitriptyline and plan an alternative pain treatment
Replace amitriptyline with clomipramine for continued pain management
Replace amitriptyline with nortriptyline for continued pain management
explanation:
**Strongly anticholinergic antidepressants** are described as sedating and capable of causing orthostatic hypotension. Amitriptyline and all three proposed substitute drugs belong to this listed group, so changing within it does not remove the stated concern (p. 2059).
"Amitriptyline Amoxapine Clomipramine Desipramine Doxepin >6 mg/day Imipramine Nortriptyline Paroxetine" (p. 2059).
"Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension;" (p. 2059).

**A. Replace amitriptyline with imipramine for continued pain management.** Wrong, Imipramine remains in the strongly anticholinergic group, so this substitution does not accomplish the stated objective (p. 2059).
**B. Discontinue amitriptyline and plan an alternative pain treatment.** Correct, removing amitriptyline while planning an alternative implements the decision to stop exposure to this strongly anticholinergic antidepressant (p. 2059).
**C. Replace amitriptyline with clomipramine for continued pain management.** Wrong, Clomipramine is also in the same strongly anticholinergic group (p. 2059).
**D. Replace amitriptyline with nortriptyline for continued pain management.** Wrong, Nortriptyline is also listed in the strongly anticholinergic group, so it does not remove the class concern (p. 2059).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2059.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING· Harrison Ch 433 — Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease

q: A 78-year-old woman has cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic heel wound. The lesion is classified as high risk. Which treatment approach does Hazzard describe for high-risk keratinocyte carcinoma?
o: Apply topical fluorouracil to the lesion as treatment of the surrounding field.
Treat the lesion with liquid nitrogen using the protocol for isolated actinic keratoses.
Apply a photosensitizing agent to the lesion and then activate it with light.
Perform Mohs micrographic surgery or surgical excision with comprehensive control of the margins.
explanation:
**High-risk keratinocyte carcinoma** requires attention to surgical margin control: Hazzard describes lower control rates when high-risk factors are present and identifies Mohs surgery or excision with comprehensive margin control as the usual treatment (p. 1460). Mohs surgery examines the surgical margins during staged removal, allowing residual tumor to be located and excised (p. 1462). "MMS is considered the gold standard for removal of high-risk keratinocyte carcinoma." (p. 1462).

**A. Apply topical fluorouracil to the lesion as treatment of the surrounding field.** Wrong, topical fluorouracil is described for fields of actinic keratoses, selected low-risk superficial basal cell carcinomas, and off-label squamous cell carcinoma in situ. That use does not supply the margin-controlled treatment described for this high-risk carcinoma (pp. 1460–1461).
**B. Treat the lesion with liquid nitrogen using the protocol for isolated actinic keratoses.** Wrong, the liquid-nitrogen protocol for isolated actinic keratoses addresses a different lesion category. The source instead directs high-risk keratinocyte carcinoma toward Mohs surgery or excision with comprehensive margin control (p. 1460).
**C. Apply a photosensitizing agent to the lesion and then activate it with light.** Wrong, this describes photodynamic therapy. Hazzard states that surgical excision is more likely to achieve complete clearance and reduce recurrence than photodynamic therapy, and identifies margin-controlled surgery for high-risk lesions (pp. 1460–1461).
**D. Perform Mohs micrographic surgery or surgical excision with comprehensive control of the margins.** Correct, the high-risk classification matches the source’s treatment recommendation. Mohs surgery uses microscopic evaluation of the entire margin and further staged excision where residual tumor is found (pp. 1460, 1462).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1460, 1461, 1462.
ref: Hazzard Ch 93 — SKIN CANCER · Harrison Ch 81 — Cancer of the Skin

q: An older woman requests an antibiotic despite the absence of a clinical indication. Which statement about treatment risks in older adults agrees with Hazzard?
o: Reduced renal function favors routine dosing because sensitivity to adverse effects is lower
Renal function and polypharmacy require attention to dose adjustment and drug interactions
Polypharmacy makes selection easier because concurrent medications reduce interaction concerns
Increasing age favors routine dosing because antibiotic adverse-effect sensitivity tends to diminish
explanation:
**Renal function and drug interactions** are important when choosing antibiotics for older adults. Hazzard states that dose adjustments are commonly needed because of reduced renal function or increased sensitivity to adverse effects (p. 1670). It also notes, "Polypharmacy can make antibiotic selection and dosing particularly challenging due to drug interactions" (p. 1670).

**A. Reduced renal function favors routine dosing because sensitivity to adverse effects is lower.** Wrong, the source connects reduced renal function with a common need for dose adjustment and describes increased, rather than reduced, sensitivity to side effects (p. 1670).
**B. Renal function and polypharmacy require attention to dose adjustment and drug interactions.** Correct, this combines the two source-described concerns: renal and adverse-effect considerations in dosing, and interactions associated with polypharmacy (p. 1670).
**C. Polypharmacy makes selection easier because concurrent medications reduce interaction concerns.** Wrong, the source says polypharmacy makes antibiotic selection and dosing more challenging because of interactions, rather than reducing those concerns (p. 1670).
**D. Increasing age favors routine dosing because antibiotic adverse-effect sensitivity tends to diminish.** Wrong, the cited discussion identifies increased sensitivity to side effects as a reason for adjustment in seniors, not a reason to assume routine dosing is suitable (p. 1670).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1670.
ref: Hazzard Ch 104 — INFECTION AND APPROPRIATE ANTIMICROBIAL SELECTION · Harrison Ch 315 — Sepsis and Septic Shock

q: מהו הטיפול המועדף בגיל המבוגר שמפחית UREMIC PRURITIS במטופל עם אי ספיקת כליות, המטופל בהמודיאליזה ?
o: GABAPENTIN במינון נמוך
CALCILESS ( POTASSIUM & SODIUM PHOSPHATE )
CIPRALEX (ESCITALOPRAM)
LYCLEAR CREAM (PERMETHRIN )
explanation:
Official answer: א

**Low-dose gabapentin** reduces uremic pruritus in hemodialysis patients, alongside optimizing dialysis, treating dry skin and addressing contributors (Hazzard p. 1296). This is a choice among the listed drugs: treatment needs renal dose adjustment and monitoring for dizziness and drowsiness, not a blanket assurance of safety (Skrzypczak et al., Gabapentinoids).
"Low-dose gabapentin has been shown to reduce uremic pruritus among patients with advanced CKD on hemodialysis." (Hazzard p. 1296).

**A. Low-dose gabapentin.** Correct, the source directly describes efficacy in the hemodialysis population. The review emphasizes dose adjustment and adverse-effect monitoring (Hazzard p. 1296; Skrzypczak et al., Gabapentinoids).
**B. Calciless (potassium and sodium phosphate).** Wrong, the preparation named in the question adds phosphate. Hazzard recommends maintaining low serum phosphate in pruritus management and dietary restriction or binders in kidney disease; supplementation does not meet that goal (pp. 1295–1296).
**C. Cipralex (escitalopram).** Wrong, the review discusses limited sertraline evidence, not specific evidence making escitalopram preferred for uremic pruritus. Evidence for one drug cannot be transferred to the entire SSRI class. This is an evidence-selection inference, not proof that escitalopram is ineffective; direct support favors gabapentin (Skrzypczak et al., antidepressant discussion; Hazzard p. 1296).
**D. Lyclear cream (permethrin).** Wrong, permethrin treats scabies infestation. When the stated diagnosis is uremic pruritus, an antiparasitic does not replace CKD-directed treatment; this indication-based inference does not exclude coexisting scabies if clinical signs warrant it (Northstar Rx, DailyMed Permethrin Cream 5%, Indications and Usage).

Inherited source-comparison note: Hazzard lists dialysis optimization, treatment of anemia and iron deficiency, low phosphate, skin moisturization, topical capsaicin and pramoxine, low-dose gabapentin and kappa-opioid receptor agonists for uremic pruritus; an SSRI is not listed (p. 1296). The prior explanation cited sertraline for PSC-associated pruritus in Harrison 22e, p. 2737. Missing step: Those sources did not explicitly address escitalopram for uremic pruritus.

Inherited source-comparison note: The topical measures in Hazzard are moisturization, capsaicin and pramoxine (p. 1296). The prior explanation cited permethrin for scabies in Harrison 22e, p. 3729, and scabies as a separate skin disease to exclude when assessing uremic pruritus in Harrison 22e, p. 2394.

These Harrison references preserve the earlier explanation and were not rechecked. The added review is not a direct study of escitalopram, so that missing step remains explicit; the choice rests on direct gabapentin evidence (Skrzypczak et al., Gabapentinoids and antidepressant discussion; Hazzard p. 1296).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1295–1296; Skrzypczak et al. Identification and Management of CKD-Associated Pruritus: Current Insights. Int J Nephrol Renovasc Dis. 2024;17:339–354, doi:10.2147/IJNRD.S499798; Northstar Rx, Permethrin Cream 5%, DailyMed label, Indications and Usage, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=11e91140-cf12-42de-9f4a-cdbc22e74658. Harrison citations above are inherited protected text, not newly checked sources.

q: מה הגישה הנכונה לטיפול תרופתי בהפרעות בהתנהגות של דמנציה?
o: רצוי להגביל בזמן את הטיפול האנטיפסיכוטי ולהפסיק כאשר התסמינים חולפים
שילוב תרופתי עדיף על טיפול יחיד להפחתת תופעות לוואי
מינון גבוה התחלתי יכול לעזור בהרגעה מהירה של המטופל
כאשר מתחילים טיפול תרופתי, הטיפול ההתנהגותי מיותר
explanation:
**Time-limited antipsychotic treatment**, with discontinuation when symptoms resolve, reflects the central caution in treating behavioral symptoms of dementia. Antipsychotics carry mortality and adverse-effect risks; start at a low dose and regularly reassess benefits and harms. The APA guidance cited on this page recommends tapering and withdrawing treatment if there is no response after four weeks, with monthly assessment during tapering and for at least four months after discontinuation (Hazzard 8e, p. 927).

**A. Limit antipsychotic duration and stop when symptoms resolve.** Correct, symptoms may resolve, so reassess the need and consider tapering and withdrawal instead of renewing treatment indefinitely (p. 927).
**B. Combining drugs is preferable to monotherapy to reduce adverse effects.** Wrong, multiple drugs can increase adverse effects and interactions; the table recommends changing one medication at a time to assess its effect (p. 927).
**C. A high starting dose can help calm the patient rapidly.** Wrong, start low and use the lowest effective dose, monitoring sedation, orthostasis, and falls (p. 927).
**D. Behavioral treatment is unnecessary once medication starts.** Wrong, the table requires concurrent nonpharmacologic interventions; prescribing does not remove the need to address behavioral triggers (p. 927).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 927, Table 60-7.

q: איזו אסטרטגיה בודדת הוכחה יעילה למניעת נפילות בקרב זקנים?
o: שימוש במכשיר שמיעה
ניתוח קטרקט
תוספת ויטמין D באנשים החיים בקהילה.
התאמת משקפיים על ידי אופטימטריסט מומחה
explanation:
Officially accepted answers: ב and ד. **Expedited cataract extraction** and provision of **single-lens glasses** to regular multifocal-glasses wearers are among single interventions that reduced falls in randomized trials. The glasses evidence concerns that targeted change, not every optometric prescription change (Hazzard 8e, p. 638).

**A. Hearing-aid use.** Wrong, hearing aids are not among the single interventions listed as reducing falls in randomized trials; this does not imply that they have no other benefit (p. 638).
**B. Cataract surgery.** Correct, accepted for official scoring. Expedited cataract extraction is among the effective single interventions listed (p. 638).
**C. Vitamin D supplementation in community-dwelling people.** Wrong, the source finds no fall-prevention benefit in community-dwelling older adults, distinguishing them from possible benefit in residential care (p. 639).
**D. Glasses fitted by an expert optometrist.** Correct, accepted for official scoring. The specific supporting intervention is single-lens distance glasses for multifocal wearers, with counseling; routine replacement with any prescription is not equivalent (pp. 638-639).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 638-639.

B. 27%: This is fall incidence in acute hospital geriatric wards (p633).

q: Why can a pressure injury cause substantial deep muscle damage before skin breakdown becomes visible?
o: The overlying skin develops irreversible injury before the deeper muscle becomes damaged.
Metabolically active ischemic muscle is especially sensitive to tissue deformation.
Restoration of perfusion after prolonged pressure brings the tissue injury process to an end.
Increased local temperature reduces tissue oxygen requirements during compression.
explanation:
**Deep tissue injury can precede visible skin damage.** Ischemic muscle is vulnerable to deformation, and local inflammation and edema can develop before the skin surface shows the injury. Heat increases oxygen demand, while reperfusion after prolonged compression can add oxidative injury (p. 681).
"Muscle tissue is metabolically active and when ischemic it is more sensitive to deformation forces" (p. 681).
"irreversible damage may be present at the muscle layer without such damage occurring in the skin or subcutaneous layers." (p. 681).

**A. The overlying skin develops irreversible injury before the deeper muscle becomes damaged.** Wrong, deep muscle can already be irreversibly damaged while skin and subcutaneous tissue lack such damage, so visible skin injury is not a prerequisite (p. 681).
**B. Metabolically active ischemic muscle is especially sensitive to tissue deformation.** Correct, the combination of high metabolic activity, ischemia, and deformation explains why muscle may be damaged before the overlying layers (p. 681).
**C. Restoration of perfusion after prolonged pressure brings the tissue injury process to an end.** Wrong, reoxygenation can release oxygen-free radicals and cause additional endothelial injury; pressure relief does not immediately terminate all tissue injury (p. 681).
**D. Increased local temperature reduces tissue oxygen requirements during compression.** Wrong, heat increases metabolic rate and therefore oxygen need, worsening the consequences of ischemia instead of protecting the tissue (p. 681).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 681.

q: An older adult has syncope attributed to symptomatic cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome. Which treatment does Hazzard identify as the treatment of choice?
o: Midodrine as used for the vasodepressor form of the syndrome
Catheter ablation as used for intrinsic cardiac tachyarrhythmias
Carotid sinus denervation before attempting the preferred therapy
Atrioventricular sequential pacing using a dual-chamber pacemaker
explanation:
**Syncope treatment** should target the identified cause. For symptomatic cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome, Hazzard states that "atrioventricular sequential (dual chamber) cardiac pacing is the treatment of choice." The chapter distinguishes this from vasodepressor disease and tachyarrhythmias, which require different treatment approaches (p. 675).

**A. Midodrine as used for the vasodepressor form of the syndrome.** Wrong, the midodrine trial discussed on this page concerns vasodepressor carotid sinus syndrome, while this patient has the cardioinhibitory form for which pacing is preferred (p. 675).
**B. Catheter ablation as used for intrinsic cardiac tachyarrhythmias.** Wrong, catheter ablation is recommended for syncope due to intrinsic tachyarrhythmias; that cause is not the one established in this stem (p. 675).
**C. Carotid sinus denervation before attempting the preferred therapy.** Wrong, the source reserves denervation as a possible option in refractory situations, so it does not replace the named treatment of choice as the initial approach (p. 675).
**D. Atrioventricular sequential pacing using a dual-chamber pacemaker.** Correct, this is the preferred treatment specifically linked to symptomatic cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome (p. 675).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 675.

q: An older adult with osteoporosis develops height loss and kyphosis without recalling severe back pain. Which interpretation is best supported?
o: The absence of severe pain makes a slowly developing vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
The height loss and kyphosis support suspicion of a slowly developing vertebral fracture.
The absence of neurological signs makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
The absence of a recalled fall makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
explanation:
**Absence of pain does not exclude vertebral fracture**, because slowly developing fractures are often asymptomatic (p. 1631). The source explains: “Height loss and kyphosis should heighten suspicion for the presence of a vertebral fracture.” (p. 1631). Inference: assessment driven only by severe pain would miss part of the fracture burden; height and posture changes provide additional clues (p. 1631).

**A. The absence of severe pain makes a slowly developing vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.** Wrong, slowly developing fractures are often asymptomatic, so lack of severe pain does not argue against that presentation (p. 1631).
**B. The height loss and kyphosis support suspicion of a slowly developing vertebral fracture.** Correct, the page identifies height loss and kyphosis as reasons for suspicion and explains that slowly developing fractures may be silent (p. 1631).
**C. The absence of neurological signs makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.** Wrong, neurological findings are rare in osteoporotic vertebral fractures because there is no dislocation; their absence is compatible with the diagnosis (p. 1631).
**D. The absence of a recalled fall makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.** Wrong, the page calls for considering vertebral fracture with or without a fall history; failure to recall a fall is not a sound reason to discount it (p. 1631).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1631.
